client.name: Bayan Foodstuff Co.
client.profile: Distributes packaged food to co-ops and groceries. Client for 3 years, growing ~10% a year. Professional finance team.

request: "We want a KD 2,500,000 Short Term Revolving Loan. Honestly, the extra headroom just makes me sleep better — better too much than too little, right?"

ratios.label: Computed working capital need
ratios.hint: 90/365 × COGS of 4.8M. This is what the operating cycle actually requires.

decisions.prompt: Build the proposal: what facility, how much, on what terms?

options.label: Short Term Revolving Loan
options.feedback: Working capital revolves with the cycle.

options.label: Term Loan
options.feedback: Working capital is not a 5-year amortising need.

options.label: Overdraft
options.feedback: A seven-figure permanent need invites hardcore OD usage.

options.label: Sight LC line
options.feedback: There is no trade transaction here to secure.

options.label: KD 1,200,000
options.feedback: Sized to the 90-day cycle the pack computed.

options.label: KD 2,500,000
options.feedback: KD 1.3M above any operational need — diversion territory.

options.label: KD 400,000
options.feedback: A third of the genuine need — he will strain within months.

options.label: KD 1,800,000
options.feedback: Splitting the difference is not credit analysis.

options.label: 90-day revolving drawdowns
options.feedback: Each drawdown matches the working capital cycle.

options.label: 12-month bullet
options.feedback: A year-long lump ignores how the cycle actually turns.

options.label: 5 years amortising
options.feedback: Long money for a 90-day need — maturity mismatch.

options.label: 30-day drawdowns
options.feedback: Shorter than the cycle — he must refinance mid-cycle every time.

decisions.prompt: Salem pushes back: "Other banks would give me the 2.5M without blinking." Your move?

options.label: Walk him through the cycle math and offer a limit review in 6 months against updated financials
options.feedback: You turned a refusal into advice. CFOs respect a banker who can show the arithmetic — and the 6-month review gives growth a legitimate path to a higher limit.

options.label: Meet him halfway at KD 1,800,000 to protect the relationship
options.feedback: Splitting the difference is not credit analysis — KD 600,000 of the limit still has no operational justification.

options.label: Approve the 2.5M but add a covenant that it's only for working capital
options.feedback: A covenant on paper doesn't restrain an over-sized revolving limit in practice — monitoring usage of 2.5M against a 1.2M need is a losing game.

options.label: Tell him to take the other banks' offer then
options.feedback: You just sent a profitable, healthy, growing client out the door over a conversation you could have won with arithmetic.

decisions.prompt: Security for the STRL?

options.label: Personal guarantees of the partners + assignment of receivables from the top 3 co-op customers
options.feedback: Owner commitment plus a claim on the strongest receivables in the book — security that maps directly onto what the facility finances.

options.label: Personal guarantees only
options.feedback: Acceptable for the client's quality — but the co-op receivables are sitting there, high-grade and assignable. Take them.

options.label: Clean
options.feedback: A seven-figure unsecured working capital line needs more justification than three good years.

options.label: 100% cash margin
options.feedback: Fully cash-covered working capital finance is a contradiction in terms.

learn: Size the STRL from the working capital cycle: (inventory days + receivable days − payable days) / 365 × COGS. The client's comfort number is not a credit basis — excess limits invite diversion.

client.name: Al Sawari Contracting Co.
client.profile: Your bid bond client — they WON the Ministry of Health clinic renovation. Contract value confirmed at KD 12,000,000 (a larger scope than originally tendered).

request: "We won! Signing is in three weeks. We need the 10% performance bond, the Ministry is offering a 20% advance against a guarantee, and we'll need about KD 800,000 of working capital to mobilise before the first progress payment lands."

ratios.label: Contract / annual revenue
ratios.hint: A transformational job — nearly three years of normal revenue in one contract. Execution risk is the whole story; control of cash flows is the bank's protection.

decisions.prompt: Build the post-award package: structure, sizing, and control.

options.label: PB + APG + STRL, approved as one package
options.feedback: One project, one credit decision — full exposure assessed together.

options.label: PB + APG only, no STRL
options.feedback: Workable, but the mobilisation gap is real and will be funded somewhere.

options.label: Single overdraft covering everything
options.feedback: Maximum cash exposure replacing controlled contingent instruments.

options.label: PB now; APG and STRL later, piecemeal
options.feedback: Nobody ever assesses the full KD 4.4M as a package.

options.label: PB 1.2M + APG 2.4M + STRL 800K
options.feedback: Exactly what the contract terms require — no more, no less.

options.label: PB 600K + APG 1.2M
options.feedback: Half what the Ministry requires — the contract cannot sign.

options.label: PB 1.2M + APG 2.4M + STRL 2.0M
options.feedback: KD 1.2M of working capital with no justification.

options.label: PB 2.4M + APG 1.2M
options.feedback: The percentages are swapped — check the contract.

options.label: Advance routed through us + assignment of proceeds
options.feedback: Every Ministry dinar lands where the bank can see it.

options.label: Advance paid wherever the client prefers
options.feedback: A KD 2.4M advance you cannot see is an advance you cannot trust.

options.label: No special routing — monitor at renewal
options.feedback: Annual hindsight is not control of live project cash.

options.label: 100% cash margin on the bonds instead
options.feedback: KD 3.6M of blocked cash would strangle the project.

decisions.prompt: Security package for KD 4.4M of project exposure?

options.label: Assignment of all contract proceeds + advance routed via the bank + 10% cash margin on the bonds + PGs of partners
options.feedback: Belt and braces: the Ministry pays us, we watch the advance, the margin cushions a call, the partners stay committed. This is how a 2.9x-revenue contract becomes bankable.

options.label: Assignment of contract proceeds only
options.feedback: The single most important element is there — but on a contract this size relative to the client, the margin and PGs are cheap insurance you shouldn't skip.

options.label: 100% cash margin on both bonds
options.feedback: KD 3.6M of blocked cash — more than the advance itself. The structure would strangle the project it's meant to enable.

options.label: Clean — they've never failed a project
options.feedback: Their six completed projects averaged a fifth of this size. Past performance at KD 2M does not collateralise KD 4.4M of exposure at 2.9x revenue.

facilitySummary: PB KD 1.2M + APG KD 2.4M + STRL KD 800K (MOH project)

plantedError.prompt: You review the deal file the day before issuance. One line in the processing history catches your eye. What's wrong?
exhibit: Credit proposal — PB KD 1.2M + APG KD 2.4M + STRL KD 800K (one package)
Call report & site visit — completed Monday
Credit analysis & risk rating — completed Tuesday
LG application sent to operations for issuance — Wednesday
Award letter and contract — on file

options.label: The LG application was sent to operations for issuance before the credit committee approved the package
options.feedback: Exactly. Nothing goes to issuance before approval — sequence is not bureaucracy, it's control. An issued guarantee is irrevocable even if the committee later declines.

options.label: The award letter is addressed to the client, not the bank
options.feedback: Award letters are always addressed to the contractor — that's normal.

options.label: Nothing — the file is in order
options.feedback: Look at the sequence: issuance was requested before committee approval. That's a serious process breach.

learn: Assess a project's facilities as one package — bonds, advance, and working capital together — and take control of the cash: assignment of proceeds and the advance routed through the bank.

client.name: Khiran Plastics Industries
client.profile: Manufactures plastic packaging. Client for 4 years. Hardworking, ambitious — sometimes more ambitious than his balance sheet.

request: "There's a German extrusion line for sale — KD 900,000, almost new. With it I can take contracts I currently turn away. I want a 5-year term loan for the full amount."

ratios.label: DSCR — as requested (900K / 5 yrs)
ratios.hint: Pre-computed: annual cash flow does not cover the proposed instalments. As requested, this loan defaults on arithmetic alone.

ratios.label: DSCR — at 600K / 6 yrs
ratios.hint: Pre-computed: a smaller loan over a longer tenor is affordable.

decisions.prompt: Build the financing for the extrusion line.

options.label: Term Loan
options.feedback: A 10-year asset is term-loan territory.

options.label: Short Term Revolving Loan
options.feedback: A machine never converts back to cash each cycle.

options.label: Overdraft
options.feedback: A permanent KD 900K hardcore from day one.

options.label: Usance LC, rolled
options.feedback: Trade paper cannot amortise capital equipment.

options.label: KD 600,000 — Waleed funds 300K himself
options.feedback: DSCR 1.3x, and his own money aligns his interests with ours.

options.label: KD 900,000 — the full price
options.feedback: DSCR 0.8x: the default is scheduled before the first instalment.

options.label: KD 300,000
options.feedback: He cannot buy the machine — the deal dies politely.

options.label: KD 750,000
options.feedback: Still beyond what his cash flow services.

options.label: 6 years
options.feedback: Comfortable coverage, well inside the machine’s life.

options.label: 5 years
options.feedback: Tight even at the smaller amount — no room for a bad quarter.

options.label: 9 years
options.feedback: Stretched to the edge of the machine’s useful life.

options.label: 12 months
options.feedback: No cash flow on earth services that schedule.

decisions.prompt: Security for the term loan?

options.label: Lien/mortgage over the extrusion line + personal guarantee
options.feedback: The financed asset plus owner commitment — the standard, proportionate package for equipment finance.

options.label: Mortgage over the factory premises
options.feedback: Strong security — arguably stronger than the machine — but heavier than the deal needs, and it consumes collateral capacity he may need for future growth.

options.label: Clean — his equity contribution is skin in the game
options.feedback: His contribution protects him from over-borrowing; it does nothing for the bank's recovery if things fail. Take the lien.

options.label: Pledge over his personal share portfolio
options.feedback: Volatile security needing margin calls and monitoring, when the machine itself is sitting there unencumbered.

plantedError.prompt: At signing, the documentation officer compares signatures. Something doesn't match. What's the issue?
exhibit: Term loan agreement KD 600,000 — signed today by the owner
Documentation note: signature on agreement slants left, thin stroke
Specimen signature card (on file since 2019): slants right, heavy stroke
Lien over extrusion line — registration initiated
Insurance over the machine — assigned to the bank

options.label: The signature on the facility agreement doesn't match the specimen signature card on file
options.feedback: Correct — stop the signing. A mismatched signature can render the agreement unenforceable. Verify identity and update the specimen card through proper channels first.

options.label: The agreement is signed in blue ink instead of black
options.feedback: Ink colour is not the issue — signature authenticity is.

options.label: Nothing — minor variations in signatures are normal
options.feedback: Variations happen, but a mismatch flagged by documentation must be resolved, never waved through.

learn: DSCR is the gate for term lending: below ~1.2x, restructure the deal — smaller amount, longer (sensible) tenor, or more client equity. The pack gives you the scenarios; your job is to pick the one that works.

client.name: Jahra Building Materials Co.
client.profile: Imports ceramic tiles and sanitary ware from Spain. Client for 3 years, decent conduct, occasionally pushes for aggressive terms.

request: "We want a usance LC line, KD 600,000, at 180 days. Long usance means we keep our cash longer — what's not to like?"

ratios.label: Inventory days
ratios.hint: Tiles sell through in two months.

ratios.label: Cash conversion of a shipment
ratios.hint: Pre-computed: 60 days to sell + 30 to collect. Cash from each shipment is in hand by day 90.

ratios.label: Requested usance vs cycle
ratios.hint: He'd hold collected cash for ~90 extra days before the LC falls due. Where does that cash sit — and what's it doing — in the meantime?

decisions.prompt: Build the trade line: instrument, size, and usance period.

options.label: Usance LC (Acceptance)
options.feedback: Deferred payment backed by the bank — built for this.

options.label: Sight LC + STRL for the gap
options.feedback: Economically equivalent, just two facilities doing one job.

options.label: Sight LC only
options.feedback: Pays at shipment and leaves a 90-day funding hole.

options.label: Term Loan
options.feedback: Five-year debt for tiles that sell in 60 days.

options.label: KD 600,000
options.feedback: Matches the import flow the pack shows.

options.label: KD 1,200,000
options.feedback: Double the documented trade — where does the rest go?

options.label: KD 300,000
options.feedback: Half his shipment flow — he will be back, irritated, in weeks.

options.label: KD 2,200,000 — full annual imports
options.feedback: A year of imports outstanding at once was never the cycle.

options.label: 90 days
options.feedback: Goods sell, cash collects, LC falls due — in that order.

options.label: 180 days — as requested
options.feedback: ~90 days of float holding money owed to a maturing obligation.

options.label: 360 days
options.feedback: Four times the cycle — pure financing of something else.

options.label: 30 days
options.feedback: Shorter than the cycle — creates the gap usance exists to close.

decisions.prompt: Talal frowns: "Gulf Premier Bank offered me 180 days, no cash margin. Match it or I move my business."

options.label: Hold the structure; show him the cycle math and explain that 90 days keeps the line self-liquidating — and cheaper
options.feedback: The competitor is mispricing risk; that's their problem. Clients respect a banker whose terms have reasons. He stayed — and so did the structure.

options.label: Compromise at 120 days
options.feedback: A modest cushion past the cycle is defensible — but be honest that it's relationship pricing, not analysis, and watch how the extra 30 days gets used.

options.label: Match the 180 days — retention first
options.feedback: You let a competitor's bad structure set your credit standards. The 90-day float problem is now yours.

options.label: Let him walk
options.feedback: There was a winnable conversation between 'surrender' and 'goodbye' — you skipped it and lost a sound, profitable trade client.

decisions.prompt: Security for the usance LC line?

options.label: 15% cash margin + personal guarantee + pledge of trust receipts over the goods
options.feedback: Margin for the first loss, PG for commitment, and the trust receipt structure keeps a legal claim on the very goods the LC financed until they're sold.

options.label: 15% cash margin + personal guarantee
options.feedback: Solid and standard — adding goods control via trust receipts would complete the trade structure.

options.label: Clean — competitive pressure demands it
options.feedback: Pricing pressure is an argument about margins, not about abandoning security on a six-figure trade line.

options.label: Mortgage over his warehouse
options.feedback: Heavy, slow security misaligned with a revolving 90-day trade line — and overkill that pushes the client toward that competitor.

learn: The usance period is a tenor — match it to the cash conversion cycle. Usance longer than the cycle hands the client a float of bank-owed money, and floats get spent.

client.name: Liyan Logistics Co.
client.profile: Last-mile distribution for retailers. Client for 2 years. Just signed two new retail distribution contracts that require more trucks.

request: "The new contracts need twenty additional trucks — KD 1,400,000. We'd like a term loan over five years; can you make it work?"

figures.label: New contracts (signed)

ratios.label: DSCR — 1.4M over 5 years
ratios.hint: Pre-computed, on current cash flow: tight. One bad quarter and instalments are missed.

ratios.label: DSCR — 1.4M over 7 years
ratios.hint: Pre-computed: comfortable, with the new contracts' cash flow as upside on top.

decisions.prompt: Build the fleet financing.

options.label: Term Loan
options.feedback: Eight-year assets, amortising debt.

options.label: Overdraft
options.feedback: KD 1.4M of trucks parked permanently on a swing line.

options.label: Short Term Revolving Loan
options.feedback: Trucks don’t convert to cash each quarter.

options.label: Invoice discounting line
options.feedback: Funds receivables, not vehicle purchases.

options.label: KD 1,400,000 — all twenty trucks
options.feedback: The contracts are signed; the capacity is needed now.

options.label: KD 1,000,000 — fourteen trucks first
options.feedback: Conservative and defensible, at some risk to the new contracts.

options.label: KD 2,000,000 — with buffer
options.feedback: KD 600K of "buffer" nobody asked to justify.

options.label: KD 500,000
options.feedback: Too few trucks to serve the contracts that justify the deal.

options.label: 7 years
options.feedback: 1.4x coverage on today’s cash flow, inside the trucks’ life.

options.label: 5 years
options.feedback: 1.1x — priced for perfection in an imperfect world.

options.label: 3 years

options.label: 10 years
options.feedback: Two years past the fleet’s useful life.

decisions.prompt: Security for KD 1.4M of fleet finance?

options.label: Mortgage/lien over the fleet + assignment of receivables from the two new retail contracts
options.feedback: The trucks secure their own loan and the contracts that justify the expansion repay it — security and repayment source pointing at the same place.

options.label: Lien over the fleet only

options.label: Personal guarantee of the CEO only

client.name: Salwa Pharma Distribution
client.profile: Licensed distributor supplying the Ministry of Health and private hospitals. Client for 4 years. Strong margins, chronically slow government receivables.

request: "The Ministry owes us KD 2,200,000 in approved invoices and pays in 120 to 150 days. Meanwhile we pay our suppliers in 60. The gap is crushing us. Can we discount the receivables?"

ratios.label: Receivable days (MOH)
ratios.hint: The gap: paid by suppliers at day 60, paid by MOH at day 135.

ratios.label: Debtor quality
ratios.hint: Payment is near-certain; only timing is uncertain. Ideal discounting material.

ratios.label: Standard advance rate
ratios.hint: Pre-computed: 70% of 2.2M ≈ KD 1.5M. The margin absorbs deductions, disputes and delays.

decisions.prompt: Build the receivables financing.

options.label: Invoice discounting line
options.feedback: Purpose-built: advance against certified government invoices.

options.label: Short Term Revolving Loan
options.feedback: Funds the same gap without harnessing the debtor’s strength.

options.label: Overdraft
options.feedback: A structural 135-day lag parked as permanent OD.

options.label: Term Loan
options.feedback: There is no five-year asset here — cash arrives in 135 days.

options.label: KD 1,500,000 (~70% advance rate)
options.feedback: The 30% margin absorbs deductions, disputes and delay.

options.label: KD 2,200,000 (100%)
options.feedback: Every routine MOH deduction now lands on the bank.

options.label: KD 700,000
options.feedback: Leaves most of the crushing gap unfunded.

options.label: KD 2,500,000 — above the book
options.feedback: Advancing more than the receivables that exist.

options.label: With recourse + assignment with MOH notification
options.feedback: The Ministry pays the bank; the client stays behind their paper.

options.label: With recourse, no notification
options.feedback: Collections detour through the client’s hands first.

options.label: Without recourse
options.feedback: The bank inherits every dispute with no claim back.

options.label: Clean advance, no assignment
options.feedback: Lending against paper the bank has no claim on.

decisions.prompt: Security for the discounting line?

options.label: Assignment of the MOH receivables with formal notification — Ministry pays the bank's account directly
options.feedback: The notification is the teeth: once MOH pays the bank directly, collections can't detour through the client. Assignment without notification is a promise; with it, it's a structure.

options.label: Assignment of receivables, no notification — client prefers MOH isn't contacted
options.feedback: Then every collection passes through the client's hands first, and in a squeeze it funds payroll before it repays the bank. The client's discomfort is the structure's whole point.

options.label: Personal guarantee of Dr. Reem
options.feedback: Recourse to the owner is fine as a supplement — as the security, it ignores the government receivable that makes this deal good.

options.label: Clean — the invoices are approved, what can go wrong
options.feedback: Approved invoices pay the client unless assigned to the bank. Clean discounting is lending against paper you have no claim on.

plantedError.prompt: Operations samples the invoice batch before the first advance. One issue surfaces. What is it?
exhibit: Invoice batch for discounting — 12 invoices, total KD 1,480,000
Invoice #4471, KD 180,000 — status: 'under review at MOH'

options.label: An invoice for KD 180,000 carries no MOH certification stamp — it's still 'under review'
options.feedback: Right. 'Under review' means it can still be disputed or reduced. Only certified invoices enter the discounting pool — exclude it until stamped.

options.label: The invoices are numbered non-sequentially
options.feedback: Clients invoice many customers; gaps in the sequence shown to us are normal.

options.label: Nothing — advance against the batch
options.feedback: One invoice is uncertified — still capable of being disputed. It must come out of the pool.

learn: In discounting, structure does the credit work: ~70% advance rate absorbs deductions, recourse keeps the client committed, and assignment WITH debtor notification makes collections flow to the bank, not through the client.

client.name: Sharq Interiors & Fit-Out Co.
client.profile: Talented, fast-growing fit-out contractor. Client for 3 years. Wins work easily; manages money chaotically. Everything runs through one overdraft.

request: "Business is booming — revenue up 45%! But the overdraft is always at the ceiling and we keep needing guarantees at the last minute for new projects. Just raise the OD from KD 1,000,000 to 1,500,000 and we're sorted."

figures.label: Overdraft usage
figures.value: KD 950,000 of 1,000,000 — at the ceiling for 9 months straight

ratios.label: Current ratio
ratios.hint: Liquidity is thinning while revenue soars — growth is consuming cash faster than profits replace it.

ratios.label: Leverage (Debt / Equity)
ratios.hint: Rising fast. The classic overtrading signature: growth funded entirely by debt.

ratios.label: OD behaviour
ratios.hint: This is not an overdraft anymore; it's permanent working capital wearing the wrong clothes.

decisions.prompt: Rebuild the facilities: approach, working capital size, and conditions.

options.label: STRL for WIP + LG line + OD trimmed to true swings
options.feedback: Each need gets its instrument; the OD becomes an OD again.

options.label: Term-out the hardcore into a 5-year TL + small OD + LG line
options.feedback: The classic hardcore cleanup — blunter than an STRL, but honest.

options.label: Raise the OD ceiling to KD 1,500,000
options.feedback: Feeding the hardcore: same chaos at a bigger number.

options.label: Freeze all lines until ratios improve
options.feedback: Strands seven live projects and likely causes the default.

options.label: KD 1,000,000 — sized to the WIP cycle
options.feedback: Project working capital, computed from the projects.

options.label: KD 1,500,000
options.feedback: The increase he asked for, wearing a new name.

options.label: KD 400,000
options.feedback: Starves seven live projects mid-build.

options.label: None — OD only
options.feedback: Recreates exactly the structure that failed.

options.label: Assignment of proceeds + quarterly management accounts
options.feedback: Control of the cash and early sight of trouble.

options.label: Personal guarantees of the partners only
options.feedback: Commitment without the cash control that matters here.

options.label: No conditions — the restructure is enough
options.feedback: Half a restructure: rebuilt and immediately unmonitored.

options.label: 100% cash margins on the LG line
options.feedback: He has no spare cash — that is the whole situation.

decisions.prompt: Looking at the pack as a whole — what is the underlying condition you're treating?

options.label: Overtrading: growth outrunning capital, visible in rising leverage, falling margins and thinning liquidity
options.feedback: Precisely. Overtrading kills profitable companies — they run out of cash while the order book is full. The cure is structure plus capital discipline, applied early.

options.label: Fraud — the growth numbers are probably fake
options.feedback: Nothing in the pack suggests fabrication — the WIP, the margins, the OD behaviour all tell one coherent (and common) story: real growth, unfunded.

options.label: Nothing — 45% growth is simply success; bankers worry too much
options.feedback: Falling margins, hardcore OD and leverage up 60% are not the texture of healthy growth. Companies overtrade their way into insolvency with full order books.

options.label: A pricing problem — he should simply raise his prices
options.feedback: Margin pressure is one symptom, but the disease is structural: growth consuming cash with no funding plan. Pricing advice doesn't fix the balance sheet.

decisions.prompt: Conditions and security for the restructured package?

options.label: Assignment of proceeds on all bonded projects + quarterly management accounts covenant + PGs of partners
options.feedback: Control of the cash, early sight of trouble, and committed owners — the monitoring package that makes lending to an overtrader survivable.

options.label: PGs of the partners only
options.feedback: Commitment, yes — but with seven live projects, the assignments of proceeds are the security that actually intercepts cash.

options.label: Existing arrangements are fine — restructuring was enough
options.feedback: You rebuilt the facilities and left them unsecured and unmonitored — half a restructure. The covenant and assignments are what keep it fixed.

options.label: 100% cash margin on the LG line
options.feedback: He has no spare cash — that's the entire situation. Full margins would simply stop the projects.

learn: A permanently maxed overdraft is a structure problem, not a limit problem. Rebuild by need — STRL for the cycle, LG line for bonds, small OD for swings — and watch for overtrading: growth that consumes cash faster than it creates it.

client.name: Bneid Al-Gar Trading Est.
client.profile: Imports and distributes household goods. Client for 6 years, historically solid. Today's request comes with financials that deserve a slow, careful read.

options.label: Increase to KD 1,200,000
options.feedback: Doubling exposure to a warehouse of unsold stock.

options.label: Increase to KD 900,000
options.feedback: Half the new money, same unanswered question.

options.label: Cut to KD 300,000 immediately
options.feedback: A reflex cut mid-cycle can trigger the very default you fear.

options.label: Detailed stock aging + warehouse visit
options.feedback: Turns suspicion into facts within a week.

options.label: Take his word — six good years
options.feedback: Relationship lending is knowing the client, not skipping the work.

options.label: Wait for next year’s audited financials
options.feedback: Twelve months of exposure to a question answerable this week.

options.label: Ask him for a budget and projections
options.feedback: Projections cannot explain stock that already isn’t selling.

options.label: Monthly stock & aging reports + pledge where feasible
options.feedback: Visibility now, claim on the asset everyone is worried about.

options.label: Quarterly financials covenant
options.feedback: Helpful but slow for a situation moving this fast.

options.label: Nothing until the review lands
options.feedback: The exposure is live today; monitoring starts today.

options.label: Demand his house or call the facility
options.feedback: An ultimatum on suspicion converts a workout into a war.

decisions.prompt: Mubarak is waiting. What's your decision on the limit?

options.label: Hold at KD 600,000; request a detailed stock aging list and a warehouse visit before considering any change
options.feedback: No new money into an unexplained inventory pile — but no panic either. The stock list and site visit turn suspicion into facts, and the relationship survives a fact-finding pause.

options.label: Approve the increase to KD 1,200,000 — six good years have earned it
options.feedback: You doubled exposure to a client whose cash is visibly buried in unsold stock. The new drawdowns will buy more of the same — and the bank now funds a warehouse of dead goods.

options.label: Split the difference — increase to KD 900,000
options.feedback: Half the new money, same unanswered question. Until the inventory mystery is explained, any increase is a guess.

options.label: Cut the limit to KD 300,000 immediately — protect the bank now
options.feedback: Yanking working capital from a client mid-cycle can trigger the very default you're guarding against. De-risk on evidence, with a managed plan — not as a reflex.

decisions.prompt: While the review runs, what do you tighten?

options.label: Monthly stock and aging reports + PG confirmation + pledge over inventory where feasible
options.feedback: Visibility first: monthly aging shows whether the stock moves, and the pledge puts the bank closer to the asset everyone is worried about.

options.label: Quarterly financials covenant
options.feedback: Helpful, but quarterly is slow for a situation moving this fast — monthly stock data is the metric that matters here.

options.label: Nothing — wait for the stock list before any changes
options.feedback: The review may take weeks; the exposure is live today. Monitoring starts now, not after the findings.

options.label: Demand his house as additional collateral or call the facility
options.feedback: An ultimatum on suspicion — before facts — converts a manageable workout into a hostile one. Escalation has an order.

learn: Inventory days exploding while sales stay flat = stock that isn't selling. The answer to 'lend more?' is 'show me the aging.' Investigate before increasing — and de-risk with a plan, not a panic.
